newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine 1996 oil product consumption up 5.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: Philippine 1996 oil product consumption up 5.8 pct.

text.p: Philippine petroleum products consumption rose by 5.8 percent to 131.6 million barrels in 1996 from 124.344 million barrels in 1995, the Department of Energy reported on Monday.
Consumption was mainly spurred by the strong petroleum demand from the transport and household sectors, the department said.

On a per product basis, usage of gasoline products, such as premium, regular and unleaded, reported the highest growth in terms of volume by 2.315 million barrels to 19.907 million barrels due to brisk sales of passenger cars.
Demand for diesel followed with a 1.721 million-barrel gain to 40.211 million from 38.490 million barrels in 1995.
"This hefty increase in gasoline and diesel usage greatly reflects the robust petroleum demand of the transport sector," the department said.
While consumption of fuel oil went down by 0.2 percent to 45.158 million barrels in 1996, it still had the biggest share of 34.3 percent of the total, the government said.
The lower demand for fuel oil was attributed to the use of more base-load, coal-fired power plants.
Demand for liquefied petroleum gas rose by 12 percent to 9.287 million barrels, fuelled by the steady increase of consumption in industrial and household sectors, the government said.
The use of aviation fuel had a 25.9 percent increase to 6.138 million barrels in 1996 due to the entry of additional domestic airline companies.
Kerosene grew by 4.5 percent to 4.563 million barrels.
Usage of non-energy products, such as alphalts, solvents, lubes and greases, rose by 4.6 percent to 2.260 million barrels.
The government also reported the country's total crude requirement in 1996 was almost 100 percent provided by imports since local crudes supplied a mere 0.4 percent.
Crude importation rose by 7.5 percent to 128.017 million barrels in 1996, of which 93 percent was supplied by the Middle East.
The net oil import bill for 1996 grew by 18 percent to $2.666 billion from $2.261 billion.
The average FOB crude cost was $19.32 per barrel, 16.2 percent higher than the $16.62 per barrel in 1995, the government said.
